title: NHS apologises and admits Palantir engineers have access to identifiable patient data

content_html:
The central health service body has acknowledged the inaccuracy of claims previously made in a transparency document which indicated that only NHS staff were able to see such sensitive information

NHS England has issued an apology after admitting that employees from Palantir and other suppliers can access identifiable information related to individual patients via the Federated Data Platform.

In its previously published Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) – a transparency document that is a statutory requirement for many public services engaged in the processing of citizens’ sensitive personal data – the NHS had claimed only health-service staff could access identifiable individual info via the FDP.

Recent reports, however, have claimed that representatives from the platform’s core supplier, Palantir, can also access this sensitive data. Following the emergence of these stories, independent adviser and scrutiniser Dr Nicola Byrne – who holds the post of National Data Guardian – wrote to the NHS requesting clarity on whether or not external contractors and supplier staff could see patient info.

In a newly published response, NHS England stressed that – outside of the inaccurate DPIA – “we have always been clear publicly and on our website that authorised users from the supplier will be granted access to data”.

But the statement from the health service went on to admit “within the DPIA we referred to only NHS England staff having access to directly identifiable patient data [but]… in fact some suppliers working for NHS England do have controlled access”.

“We recognise that the DPIA contained an error in how it described supplier access to data so we are correcting that error, and we apologise for any confusion this has caused,” the NHS said.

Access is provided via the FDP’s National Data Integration Tenant system, as part of supporting which three Palantir engineers “currently have administrative-level access to the NDIT”, while “a further 33 engineers from a variety of suppliers have more limited project-specific access to work on specific data sets and tasks assigned by NHS England including writing code and assuring the development of new products”.

“In all cases they do not have permission to use the data for their own purposes – their role is strictly limited to supporting the safe running and maintenance of the platform,” the health service added. “The access is granted based on operational need and is time limited therefore the numbers can fluctuate over time. Within NDIT, engineers, operating under the instruction of NHS England, could access identifiable and de-identifiable patient data, however this would only be to provide specific technical support – patient data is not routinely accessed.”

In response to the NHS clarification, data guardian Dr Byrne said that she and her team will “continue to engage with the programme in our independent advisory role, providing advice on its documentation, transparency materials… [and] will continue to provide challenge where necessary, and advocate for practices that build and maintain public and professional trust”.

She added that “we continue to strongly support the programme’s ambition” – but acknowledged the prevalence and vehemence of concerns regarding the FDP, and the presence of its primary tech supplier.

“The intensity of interest and strength of public feeling on this issue appear to reflect not only how deeply many people care about the use of their data, and its confidentiality, but also continuing concern amongst some about Palantir’s role in the NHS,” Byrne said. “This topic has always been to some extent political. As such, people have a range of views. And public, professional and media scrutiny has only increased over time. This means that accuracy and transparency must remain central priorities for the NHS FDP programme. This incident has shown how quickly confidence erodes if the ‘no surprises’ principle [of NHS data use] is not upheld when it comes to who can access people’s data, and why.”

MPs on the Science, Innovation and Technology Committee recently issued a report stating that “Palantir shouldn’t play such a significant role in the UK public sector”, and naming the vendor “as the most concerning example of the public sector’s growing reliance on a small number of major technology providers, [also] including Microsoft and Amazon Web Services”.

The committee issued unequivocal guidance that government should exercise a break clause enabling the NHS to exit the FDP engagement in March 2027 – and should then “either develop an in-house replacement or seek an alternative UK provider”.

content_html_zh:
中央卫生服务机构承认之前在一份透明度文件中提出的说法不准确，该文件表明只有 NHS 工作人员才能看到此类敏感信息

英国 NHS 在承认 Palantir 和其他供应商的员工可以通过联合数据平台访问与个体患者相关的身份信息后发表了道歉。

NHS 在其之前发布的数据保护影响评估 (DPIA) 中（一份透明度文件，是许多参与处理公民敏感个人数据的公共服务机构的法定要求）声称，只有医疗服务人员可以通过 FDP 访问可识别的个人信息。

然而，最近的报道称，该平台核心供应商 Palantir 的代表也可以访问这些敏感数据。 这些故事出现后，担任国家数据卫士的独立顾问和审查员 Nicola Byrne 博士写信给 NHS，要求澄清外部承包商和供应商工作人员是否可以看到患者信息。

在新发布的回应中，英国 NHS 强调，除了不准确的 DPIA 之外，“我们一直在公开场合和我们的网站上明确表示，供应商的授权用户将被授予访问数据的权限”。

但卫生服务部门的声明接着承认，“在 DPIA 中，我们提到只有 NHS 英格兰工作人员有权访问直接可识别的患者数据 [但是]…… 事实上，一些为英国国民医疗服务体系（NHS England）工作的供应商确实拥有受控的访问权限”。

NHS 表示：“我们认识到 DPIA 在描述供应商访问数据的方式上存在错误，因此我们正在纠正该错误，对于由此造成的任何混乱，我们深表歉意。”

  • 政府将花费高达 2000 万英镑与中央情报局支持的大数据公司 Palantir 签署“边境流动”合同

访问权限是通过 FDP 的国家数据集成租户系统提供的，作为支持的一部分，三名 Palantir 工程师“目前拥有对 NDIT 的管理级访问权限”，而“来自不同供应商的另外 33 名工程师拥有更有限的项目特定访问权限，可以处理英格兰 NHS 分配的特定数据集和任务，包括编写代码和确保新产品的开发”。

“在所有情况下，他们都无权将数据用于自己的目的——他们的作用严格限于支持平台的安全运行和维护，”卫生服务部门补充道。 “访问权是根据运营需要授予的，并且有时间限制，因此数量可能会随着时间的推移而波动。 在 NDIT 内，工程师在英国 NHS 的指导下可以访问可识别和不可识别的患者数据，但这只是为了提供特定的技术支持——患者数据不会被定期访问。”

针对 NHS 的澄清，数据监护人 Byrne 博士表示，她和她的团队将“继续以独立咨询角色参与该计划，就其文件、透明度材料提供建议……[并且]将继续在必要时提出挑战，并倡导建立和维持公众和专业信任的做法”。

她补充说，“我们继续大力支持该计划的雄心”，但也承认人们对 FDP 及其主要技术供应商的存在存在普遍而强烈的担忧。

Byrne 表示：“公众对这个问题的兴趣和感受的强度似乎不仅反映出有多少人非常关心他们的数据的使用及其保密性，而且还反映出一些人对 Palantir 在 NHS 中的作用的持续担忧。” “这个话题在某种程度上一直是政治性的。 因此，人们有各种各样的观点。 随着时间的推移，公众、专业人士和媒体的监督有增无减。 这意味着准确性和透明度必须仍然是 NHS FDP 计划的核心优先事项。 这一事件表明，如果在谁可以访问人们的数据以及为什么访问人们的数据时不坚持[NHS数据使用]的‘不出意外’原则，信心就会迅速受到侵蚀。”

科学、创新和技术委员会的议员们最近发布了一份报告，指出“Palantir 不应该在英国公共部门发挥如此重要的作用”，并将该供应商称为“公共部门日益依赖少数主要技术提供商（还包括微软和亚马逊网络服务）的最令人担忧的例子”。

该委员会发布了明确的指导意见，要求政府应行使中断条款，使 NHS 在 2027 年 3 月退出 FDP 参与，然后“要么开发内部替代品，要么寻求替代的英国提供商”。
